cards.front: What distinguishes the preferred and null directions of a direction-selective retinal ganglion cell (DSGC)?
cards.back: Preferred motion evokes a strong response; motion in the opposite, null direction evokes little or no response.
cards.quote: fires strongly to motion in one direction, its preferred direction, and little or not at all to motion the opposite way, its null direction.
cards.section: What the mechanism must do: a veto on the null direction

cards.front: In Barlow and Hill's rabbit recordings, did replacing a light spot with a black spot change the preferred motion direction, and what did this establish?
cards.back: No. The preferred direction did not depend on whether the spot was lighter or darker than its background.
cards.quote: Replacing a light spot with a black spot kept the same preferred direction,
cards.section: What the mechanism must do: a veto on the null direction

cards.front: An ON-OFF direction-selective retinal unit responds to light {{c1::onset and offset}}.
cards.quote: ON-OFF direction-selective units, which respond both when light comes on and when it goes off,
cards.section: What the mechanism must do: a veto on the null direction

cards.front: In a retinal two-flash test using baseline-subtracted responses in matched windows, the response remainder equals the paired response minus {{c1::the sum of the single-flash responses}}.
cards.back: A negative remainder indicates net suppression; a positive remainder indicates net enhancement.
cards.quote: The useful number is the remainder, the paired response minus the sum of the singles:
cards.section: What the mechanism must do: a veto on the null direction

cards.front: What operation did Barlow and Levick infer from rabbit ON-OFF cells responding far below the single-flash sum in the null order, but near it in the preferred order?
cards.back: A local veto of null-direction sequences, operating in small subunits across the receptive field.
cards.quote: They also inferred that the veto works in small subunits spread across the receptive field, not once for the whole cell.
cards.section: What the mechanism must do: a veto on the null direction

cards.front: A retinal ganglion cell prefers upward motion. In the simple offset model, which side should supply inhibition that vetoes null motion, and why?
cards.back: The upper side: null motion travels downward and approaches from above, recruiting inhibition early enough to overlap excitation.
cards.quote: the inhibition should come from the side that null-direction motion approaches from.
cards.section: What the mechanism must do: a veto on the null direction

cards.front: In a hypothetical retinal two-flash test, baseline-subtracted singles give 4 spikes each. Matched-window pairs give 14 spikes in one order and 2 in the reverse. Calculate both remainders and interpret them.
cards.back: Additive prediction = 4 + 4 = 8 spikes. Remainders: 14 − 8 = +6 spikes, net enhancement; 2 − 8 = −6 spikes, net suppression.
cards.quote: 2 − 8 = −6 for the veto and 14 − 8 = +6 for the boost.
cards.section: What the mechanism must do: a veto on the null direction

cards.front: Why can sufficiently early inhibition veto excitation during null-direction motion in a retinal offset model?
cards.back: Inhibition cancels excitation while they overlap in time. Preferred motion reaches excitation first, giving it a head start.
cards.quote: Inhibition cancels excitation only while the two overlap in time.
cards.section: What the mechanism must do: a veto on the null direction

cards.front: Which two transmitters do starburst amacrine cells release, and what effects do they have in the retinal circuit?
cards.back: GABA inhibits; acetylcholine excites.
cards.quote: an interneuron that releases both GABA, which inhibits, and acetylcholine, which excites.
cards.section: The circuit in one picture

cards.front: In the basic retinal direction-selectivity circuit, a ganglion cell receives its excitation mainly from {{c1::bipolar cells}}.
cards.back: In this simplified picture, excitation is about the same for either direction.
cards.quote: The DSGC's excitation comes mainly from bipolar cells, and in this picture it is about the same for either direction.
cards.section: The circuit in one picture

cards.front: A starburst amacrine dendrite is most active and releases most GABA during {{c1::outward motion, from soma toward tip}}.
cards.quote: when motion runs outward, from the cell body to its tip.
cards.section: The circuit in one picture

cards.front: How do starburst branch tuning and selective wiring together suppress a retinal ganglion cell's null response?
cards.back: The strongest inhibitory branches point roughly in the ganglion cell's null direction. Null motion runs outward along them, maximizing inhibition that overlaps and vetoes excitation.
cards.quote: A direction-selective ganglion cell is wired mainly to the starburst dendrites that point in its null direction.
cards.section: The circuit in one picture

cards.front: A retinal ganglion cell prefers upward motion. A starburst soma lies above it, with a branch pointing downward over its dendrites. Which motion should evoke stronger inhibition, and why?
cards.back: Downward motion: it runs outward along the downward-pointing branch, which points in the ganglion cell's null direction and is expected to connect strongly.
cards.quote: Remember the sign: the dendrites that give a DSGC its strongest inhibition prefer roughly the direction the DSGC ignores.
cards.section: The circuit in one picture

cards.front: Suppose a starburst soma simply sums equal signals from opposite dendrites, each preferring outward motion. What directional preference should the soma show, and why?
cards.back: Little or none: motion outward along one branch is inward along its opposite, so their preferences cancel under equal summation.
cards.quote: motion that runs outward along one branch runs inward along the branch opposite it, so the preferences cancel.
cards.section: Each branch is its own detector (2002)

cards.front: What contrast between dendritic calcium and somatic voltage did Euler and colleagues find in ON starburst cells in isolated rabbit retina?
cards.back: Dendritic calcium preferred outward motion; somatic voltage lacked that preference under the tested conditions. This supports branch-level computation, without proving summation caused the somatic result.
cards.quote: Euler and colleagues found that the somatic voltage did not show the dendrites' directional preference under the conditions tested;
cards.section: Each branch is its own detector (2002)

cards.front: A simplified retinal circuit keeps its null-aligned starburst synapses, but branch release becomes identical for inward and outward motion. Excitation and input timing are equal across directions. Can selective wiring alone preserve direction selectivity?
cards.back: No. The circuit rule requires both branch tuning and selective wiring. With direction-independent release and no directional difference in excitation or timing, null-aligned contacts alone cannot create different responses to opposite motion.
cards.quote: Each branch has its own, set by where the branch points.
cards.section: Each branch is its own detector (2002)

cards.front: In a retinal ablation assay, removing a neuron population eliminates direction selectivity and the tested eye-following reflex. What causal conclusion follows?
cards.back: The population is necessary in that assay. Ablation does not establish sufficiency or identify which of the population's transmitters mediates the effect.
cards.quote: This is necessity in that assay, and taking the whole population away removes both of its transmitters together.
cards.section: Each branch is its own detector (2002)

cards.front: What functional evidence linked starburst output to the null-direction veto in Fried and colleagues' rabbit paired recordings?
cards.back: Null-pointing starburst processes delivered inhibition; preferred-pointing processes did not. Starburst inhibition was stronger during null-direction motion.
cards.quote: SAC processes pointing in a DSGC's null direction delivered inhibition and those pointing in its preferred direction did not,
cards.section: Reading the wiring (2002, 2011)

cards.front: Why did Briggman and colleagues measure mouse ganglion cells' preferred directions before reconstructing the same tissue by electron microscopy?
cards.back: Function supplied each cell's preferred and null directions, allowing branch orientation and reconstructed contacts to be related to its direction preference.
cards.quote: A wiring diagram alone does not say which way a ganglion cell prefers, so they read function first.
cards.section: Reading the wiring (2002, 2011)

cards.front: An adult retinal reconstruction shows more inhibitory contacts of one orientation. Can this alone establish stronger inhibitory conductance or developmental pruning? What evidence is missing?
cards.back: Neither conclusion follows. The anatomy rule treats contacts as indirect connectivity measures, not conductance; the snapshot rule cannot establish development. Functional measurements and recordings across developmental stages would address those gaps.
cards.quote: Anatomy does not measure the strength of a synapse, so a contact count or area is an indirect sign of connectivity, not a conductance.
cards.section: Reading the wiring (2002, 2011)

cards.front: How did Wei and colleagues' mouse paired recordings distinguish strengthening from pruning during development of starburst-to-ganglion inhibition?
cards.back: Initially similar inhibition became asymmetric as null-side inhibition grew. Preferred-side inhibition stayed about constant and persisted in adults, supporting strengthening rather than deletion.
cards.quote: Development strengthened one side and did not delete the other.
cards.section: Built by strengthening, not pruning (2011)

cards.front: Mouse direction selectivity developed despite muscimol or gabazine treatment during formation of inhibitory asymmetry. Does this show that neural activity never matters for wiring?
cards.back: No. It supports activity-independent null-side strengthening within the tested treatment window; it does not establish independence from every activity pattern at every developmental stage.
cards.quote: does not depend on neural activity, at least within that treatment window.
cards.section: Built by strengthening, not pruning (2011)

cards.front: During mouse null-side connection growth, quantal inhibitory events became more frequent without becoming larger. Why does this alone fail to prove that synapse number increased?
cards.back: By the quantal interpretation rule, frequency can increase through more release sites or higher release probability. Unchanged size argues against larger single events; additional tests are needed to distinguish the frequency mechanisms.
cards.quote: More frequent events can mean more release sites or a higher release probability, so frequency alone does not settle it.
cards.section: Built by strengthening, not pruning (2011)

cards.front: After SAC-specific reduction of GABA release in mouse retina, inhibition lost direction tuning, yet some ON-OFF ganglion cells remained direction selective. What limits the conclusion?
cards.back: Tuned inhibition is not indispensable in every tested cell: tuned excitation and relative timing can support residual selectivity. The manipulation did not eliminate all starburst GABA.
cards.quote: So direction tuning of inhibition is important but not indispensable for selectivity in every tested cell.
cards.section: Where the idea stops

cards.front: How can inhibition of equal size in both motion directions still help produce a direction-selective retinal response?
cards.back: Its timing relative to excitation can differ by direction, changing how much excitation it cancels even when inhibitory amplitude is untuned.
cards.quote: which can change how much it cancels even when its size is the same in both directions.
cards.section: Where the idea stops

cards.front: Why does similar preferred-direction enhancement and null-direction suppression in fly and mouse vision support convergent computation rather than homology?
cards.back: Different cell types implement a similar algorithm: fly T4 and T5 cells versus the mammalian starburst circuit. Algorithmic similarity alone does not establish homology.
cards.quote: The fly and the mouse reach a similar algorithm with different cells, so this is convergent computation, not homology,
cards.section: Where the idea stops

cards.front: What is the evidence limit for the candidate human counterpart of the macaque direction-selective cell described in the retinal studies?
cards.back: The human cell was identified as a candidate homolog, without a human motion recording.
cards.quote: The 2023 human cell was identified as a candidate homolog without a human motion recording.
cards.section: Where the idea stops

cards.front: For a retinal dendritic response, normalize outward response Rout to 1 and set inward response Rin to 0.32. Calculate D = (Rout − Rin)/(Rout + Rin) and interpret its sign.
cards.back: D = (1 − 0.32)/(1 + 0.32) = 0.68/1.32 ≈ 0.515. The positive sign indicates an outward preference.
cards.quote: For this exercise only, normalise the outward response to 1 and define D = (Rout - Rin) / (Rout + Rin).
cards.section: Worked problem (a): a direction index from a published ratio

cards.front: An imaging report averages inward/outward ratios from 36 dendritic regions on one cell. Can transforming that mean ratio yield a mean per-region direction index or evidence from 36 independent cells?
cards.back: Neither. By the nonlinear-transformation rule, the index of the mean ratio need not equal the mean of individual indices. By the sampling rule, regions on one cell are not separate cells or animals.
cards.quote: because the formula is non-linear it is not the mean of per-region indices, which would need each region's own ratio.
cards.section: Worked problem (a): a direction index from a published ratio

cards.front: When can a threefold ratio of inhibitory current amplitudes be interpreted as a threefold inhibitory conductance ratio?
cards.back: When inhibitory reversal potential is the same and adequate voltage clamp holds both measurements at one voltage away from that reversal, giving the same driving force.
cards.quote: the driving force is then the same, so the threefold current ratio is a threefold conductance ratio,
cards.section: Worked problem (b): when does a spike threshold sharpen the signal?

cards.front: In a passive steady-state neuron with no injected current, voltage is the average of reversal potentials weighted by {{c1::their conductances}}.
cards.back: V = (g_E E_E + g_I E_I + g_L E_L)/(g_E + g_I + g_L).
cards.quote: when the voltage is steady and no current is injected, it sits at the average of the reversal potentials, weighted by each conductance.
cards.section: Worked problem (b): when does a spike threshold sharpen the signal?

cards.front: In a passive steady-state retinal model, E_E = 0 mV, E_I = −70 mV, E_L = −60 mV; g_E = 2 and g_L = 1. With no injected current, calculate V for g_I = 1 (preferred) and 3 (null).
cards.section: Worked problem (b): when does a spike threshold sharpen the signal?

cards.front: A passive retinal model gives preferred V = −32.5 mV, null V = −45 mV and leak reversal −60 mV. Calculate (P − N)/(P + N) for depolarizations from leak. Why use depolarizations?
cards.back: P = −32.5 − (−60) = 27.5 mV; N = −45 − (−60) = 15 mV. Index = 12.5/42.5 ≈ 0.29. The index is intended for nonnegative quantities, not raw negative membrane potentials.
cards.quote: The depolarizations from the leak potential, 27.5 and 15 mV, give (27.5 − 15) / (27.5 + 15) = 12.5 / 42.5 = 0.29.
cards.section: Worked problem (b): when does a spike threshold sharpen the signal?

cards.front: In a retinal threshold model, rate is proportional to max(V − T, 0). Preferred V is −32.5 mV and null V is −45 mV. Which thresholds T give preferred firing but a silent null response, and why?
cards.back: −45 mV ≤ T < −32.5 mV. Null voltage is then at or below threshold while preferred voltage remains above it. At or above −32.5 mV both rates vanish and their direction index is undefined.
cards.quote: only for thresholds from −45 mV up to just below −32.5 mV.
cards.section: Worked problem (b): when does a spike threshold sharpen the signal?

cards.front: Let rate = max(V − T, 0) in arbitrary units, with preferred V = −32.5 mV and null V = −45 mV. At T = −55 mV, calculate the spike index (P − N)/(P + N). Does it exceed an inhibitory index magnitude of 0.50?
cards.back: Rates: P = 22.5, N = 10. Spike index = (22.5 − 10)/(22.5 + 10) = 12.5/32.5 ≈ 0.38, below 0.50. A low threshold need not sharpen selectivity relative to inhibition.
cards.quote: With a low threshold, the spike output (0.38 at −55 mV) is less selective than the inhibition (0.50).
cards.section: Worked problem (b): when does a spike threshold sharpen the signal?

cards.front: Removing retinal neurons that release both GABA and acetylcholine eliminates direction selectivity. Design a more specific test of the GABA contribution and state what a reduced but nonzero direction preference would mean.
cards.back: Reduce only their GABA release while preserving cells and acetylcholine, and compare with acute reversible cell silencing. By the transmitter-specific necessity rule, reduced preference implicates GABA; residual preference permits other contributions. Loss-of-function alone does not establish sufficiency.
cards.quote: Remove or reduce GABA release from SACs while leaving the cells and their cholinergic output in place,
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: A genetic manipulation begun before retinal circuit maturation weakens adult direction selectivity. How would you distinguish a developmental wiring effect from an adult signalling requirement?
cards.back: Compare an early manipulation with one begun in adulthood. The developmental-versus-adult rule separates altered wiring from disrupted signalling; acute reversible silencing provides a comparison less entangled with development.
cards.quote: a manipulation in the adult changes signalling. The two answer different questions.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Does a negative baseline-subtracted remainder in a retinal two-flash test uniquely identify an inhibitory veto mechanism?
cards.back: No. It measures net suppression, not a unique cellular mechanism. An opponent multiplicative detector with a linear term can also produce a deficit.
cards.quote: It does not, on its own, assign a cell to one scheme or identify a cellular mechanism.
cards.section: Veto, boost, and what the two-flash test measures

cards.front: In the linear, otherwise symmetric starburst model, contacts broaden from a single null-pointing orientation to a half-circle centred on null (±90°). Must directional inhibition disappear, and why?
cards.back: No. The model retains stronger null inhibition with loose null-centred wiring. A half-circle still favours null-pointing branches; cancellation occurs when every branch direction is sampled equally.
cards.quote: In this linear, otherwise symmetric model the last row carries no direction signal, as for a summing soma,
cards.section: How selective must the wiring be?

cards.front: What proximal-versus-distal excitatory response pattern did Fransen and Borghuis measure in mouse ON and OFF starburst cells?
cards.back: Distal excitation was faster and more transient than proximal excitation in both cell types.
cards.quote: Distal excitation was faster and more transient than proximal excitation in both types.
cards.section: Input kinetics onto the starburst dendrite

cards.front: For a pure-delay exercise in mouse starburst cells, take 26 ms per 100 micrometres for OFF cells and 8 ms per 100 micrometres for ON cells. Calculate matching speeds in micrometres per second and, using 31 micrometres per degree, degrees per second.
cards.back: Speed = distance/delay. OFF: 100/0.026 ≈ 3,800 micrometres/s, or roughly 120°/s after dividing by 31. ON: 100/0.008 = 12,500 micrometres/s, roughly 400°/s. These are exercise estimates, not measured preferred speeds.
cards.quote: A pure delay line makes the signals coincide when the stimulus crosses 100 micrometres in the delay time.
cards.section: Worked problem: a delay-line speed, and why it misleads

cards.front: Treating starburst input time-to-peak gradients as pure delays predicts much faster motion than a sustained/transient input model's low-speed regime. Does this refute a contribution from input kinetics?
cards.back: No. By the response-shape rule, a time-to-peak gradient need not be a pure delay. Sustained proximal and transient distal responses can contribute differently. The mismatch tests the pure-delay assumption, not all kinetic mechanisms.
cards.quote: The mismatch comes from the pure-delay assumption, which ignores the difference in response shape (sustained proximal, transient distal),
cards.section: Worked problem: a delay-line speed, and why it misleads

cards.front: Why is it premature to assume that glutamatergic input to mouse direction-selective ganglion cells is always direction tuned?
cards.back: Studies disagree: some report tuned and untuned input; direct glutamate imaging found no tuning, whose authors argued that apparent voltage-clamp tuning came from poor voltage control during null inhibition.
cards.quote: Park and colleagues (2014) imaged glutamate arriving on ON-OFF DSGC dendrites in mouse and found no direction tuning,
cards.section: Tuned excitation: the debate

cards.front: Which cortical motion bias was lost after disruption of retinal direction selectivity in the mouse study by Hillier and colleagues?
cards.back: The over-representation of posterior-motion-preferring layer 2/3 cells in V1; other cortical motion computations persisted.
cards.quote: disrupting retinal direction selectivity abolished the over-representation of posterior-motion-preferring layer 2/3 cells in primary visual cortex (V1), while other cortical motion computations persisted.
cards.section: Downstream: what the cortex inherits
